name: Media Arts, Photography, and Film
title: Media Arts, Photography, and Film
answer: Media arts, photography, and film classes already use digital tools with built-in AI features, such as photo editors that remove objects or change backgrounds and video editors that generate captions or suggest cuts. These features can help students realize their creative vision faster, but the authorship rule still applies: fixing lighting or removing a stray object is like any editing tool, while replacing most of a photograph with generated content changes whose work it is. Media arts is also a good place to teach about manipulated images, because students who learn how easily a photo can be altered become better at spotting altered images elsewhere.

crumbs.name: Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health

sections.body: Media arts classes already use digital tools, and AI features are now built into many of them. Photo editing software can remove objects, change backgrounds, or sharpen images with a click, and video editors can generate captions, suggest cuts, or create effects. These features can help students realize their creative vision faster. The problem is that using them raises a question about authorship, because some uses are ordinary editing and others replace the student's own work with generated content. Teachers need clear expectations about which AI features are allowed for each project.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In media arts classes, teachers should set clear expectations about which AI features are allowed for each project. Using a tool to fix lighting or remove a stray object is treated much like using any editing tool. Replacing most of a photograph with generated content changes whose work it is, so that use is treated differently. Media arts is also a good place to teach about manipulated images, connecting to the misinformation lessons in Chapter 9 and the deepfake rules in Chapter 3. A student who has made a convincing fake, with permission and for learning, understands why fakes are dangerous.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or finding for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research, drawing on how media arts classes already use digital tools and on the authorship rule applied with some nuance.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The authorship rule still applies, with some nuance. Using a tool to fix lighting or remove a stray object is much like using any editing tool, but replacing most of a photograph with generated content changes whose work it is. Teachers should set clear expectations about which AI features are allowed for each project. The decision about what is allowed stays with the teacher, and any student work with convincing fakes should be done with permission and for learning.
